summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would provide additional funding for ordinary annual Commonwealth government services in 2022-23, reflecting decisions made after the October budget for that financial year.

It would authorise scheduled departmental, administered and corporate entity spending through withdrawals from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, supplementing existing supply and appropriation legislation.
The appropriations would take effect at Royal Assent alongside separate bills for other services and parliamentary departments, without adding an advance to the Finance Minister.
changes: Departmental funding could cover spending related to an entity's functions, including staff and operational costs.
Administered funding would be allocated separately to each specified outcome.
Matching-purpose appropriations could be credited to special accounts.
The appropriation legislation would repeal at the start of 1 July 2025.
summary.affected: Non-corporate Commonwealth entities, corporate Commonwealth entities and Commonwealth companies receiving the appropriated amounts are affected.

divisions.question: The majority voted against adding the text below to the usual second reading motion, which is "*that the bills be read a second time*". To read the bills a second time is to agree with the bills' main idea. The motion was introduced by WA Senator [Dorinda Cox](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/wa/dorinda_cox) (Greens). ### Amendment text > *At the end of the motion, add ", but the Senate notes that Labor's second Budget:* > >> *(a) gives a $24.85 a day tax cut to politicians and billionaires, but only $2.85 a day to jobseekers;* >> >> *(b) gives $16.8 billion over the forward estimates in handouts to wealthy property moguls, but no new money for direct investment in new social and affordable housing;* >> >> *(c) includes $41 billion over the forward estimates in fossil fuel subsidies, which is more than all the investment in Australia becoming a renewable energy superpower; and* >> >> *(d) is a betrayal of the people who were promised that no one would be left behind".*

speeches.speaker: Carol Brown
speeches.brief: Documents on proposed expenditure for 2023‑24 and additional expenditure for 2022‑23 were tabled, and a motion was passed to refer them, together with the final budget outcome for 2021‑22 and advances under annual Appropriation Acts, to committees for examination and report.
